t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This session is devoted to detecting the arsenic cation, destruction of the liver and kidney, and analysis of mercury in the destruction product. Aim: to become familiar with the toxicological significance and analytical methods for the arsenic cation, that is, a metallic poison isolated from a biological object by mineralisation. In the DVSSM course package this session is called "detection of arsenic and mercury cations, destruction, mercury in the destruction product".

By the end of the session we will achieve three outcomes. The first: detection of the arsenic cation by the Sanger–Black method. The second: detection of the arsenic cation by the Marsh method. The third: destruction of the liver and kidney with sulphuric and nitric acids and detection of mercury in the destruction product. That is, you will master two methods for arsenic, and destruction and analysis for mercury.

The following are needed for the work: the mineralisate, Sanger–Black and Marsh apparatus, filter paper, a funnel, reagents, test tubes, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For destruction, 300 ml flasks, a boiling water bath and a 200 ml volumetric flask are used. Remember the volumes according to these sizes.

This is the session map. Arsenic is detected in the mineralisate by the Sanger–Black and Marsh methods. In the Sanger–Black method, copper-coated zinc, SnCl2 and H2SO4 are used, and the HgBr2 paper turns yellow-brown. In the Marsh method, arsine gives a bluish-green flame, and a mirror and white crystals form. For mercury, the liver and kidney are destroyed with concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3. In the destruction product, mercury is determined by the nephelometric method, with copper(I) iodide, and by the photometric method in the presence of dithizone.

In the Sanger–Black method the apparatus is assembled first. 2 ml of mineralisate is poured into the apparatus, and 10 ml of 4N H2SO4, 5 ml of water and 1 ml of SnCl2 are added; the SnCl2 is 10% and dissolved in concentrated H2SO4. Then 2 g of copper-coated zinc pieces are dropped in and the apparatus is closed with a stopper.

Indicator paper is used in the Sanger–Black method. Cotton wool impregnated with lead acetate solution is placed in the initial part of the apparatus. Then filter paper impregnated with HgBr2, or HgCl2, is placed and left for 30–40 minutes. If arsenic is present, the paper is stained from yellow to brown. If no colour appears, the examination is stopped.

The key values of the Sanger–Black method. 2 ml of mineralisate is poured into the apparatus, and 10 ml of 4N H2SO4, 5 ml of water and 1 ml of 10% SnCl2 in concentrated H2SO4 are added. 2 g of copper-coated zinc pieces are dropped in and the apparatus is closed with a stopper. Then the cotton wool and the mercury(II) bromide paper are placed and left for 30–40 minutes.

Now the Marsh method. In the Marsh apparatus, 10 g of copper-coated zinc pieces are placed in the reaction flask. The calcium chloride tube is filled with anhydrous calcium chloride crystals, all parts of the apparatus are assembled and mounted on a stand. 50 ml of 4N H2SO4 is poured into the dropping funnel and added slowly, drop by drop, to the reaction flask.

Displacing air from the apparatus is an important stage. The hydrogen being released displaces air from the apparatus for 15–20 minutes. A thin inverted test tube is placed over the end of the tube, and a burning flame is brought to its mouth. If the test tube is filled with pure hydrogen, the hydrogen burns silently; otherwise a noisy explosion occurs.

The key values of the Marsh method. 10 g of copper-coated zinc is placed in the reaction flask, and 50 ml of 4N H2SO4 is poured into the dropping funnel. Hydrogen displaces air for 15–20 minutes. The purity of the reagents is checked by the absence of a mirror after 1 hour. For the mineralisate, 1 ml of SnCl2 is added to 20 ml of mineralisate and it is added dropwise over one hour.

t: Checking the purity of the reagents
n: Checking the purity of the reagents. Once it is certain that hydrogen is being released fully, the apparatus is covered with a towel and the hydrogen coming out of the tube is ignited. The thin part of the tube is cooled with a gauze wick, while the wider part before it is heated with a small flame. After one hour, no brown-grey mirror should form in the cooled part. The absence of a mirror shows that the reagents are pure from the forensic chemical point of view.

Now we examine the mineralisate. 1 ml of SnCl2 in concentrated H2SO4 is added to 20 ml of mineralisate, and it is transferred to the dropping funnel. The mixture is added slowly, drop by drop, to the reaction flask over one hour. During this time the thin part of the reduction tube is cooled, and the thick part is kept heated.

Signs of arsine. If arsine, AsH3, forms as a result of the reaction, a bluish-green flame appears at the end of the reduction tube and a smell of garlic or onion is noticed. If a cold porcelain dish is held in the burning bluish-green flame, a shiny grey mirror forms. If the tube is carefully turned through 180° and its end is held in an ammoniacal silver nitrate solution, black turbidity appears. These are the four signs of arsenic.

Testing arsine with silver nitrate. The reduction tube is carefully turned through 180° and its end is held in an ammoniacal silver nitrate solution. When arsine is released from the tube, black turbidity begins to appear in the solution, which indicates that arsine is being released. After one hour the tube is examined: it is determined whether a shiny grey mirror is present in the thin part.

Sublimation of the arsenic mirror. The shiny mirror is heated with a small flame, and the area slightly above it is cooled with a wick soaked in cold water. The shiny mirror disappears, and white deposits form in the cooled part. Under the microscope the white deposits appear as crystals in the form of octahedra and tetrahedra. These crystals confirm arsenic.

t: Examining the deposit in the tube
n: The procedure for examining the deposit in the tube. After one hour the flame is extinguished, and once the tube has cooled, the shiny grey mirror in the thin part is examined. The mirror is heated with a small flame and the area above it is cooled with a wick with cold water, and white deposits then form. Under the microscope they are observed as crystals in the form of octahedra and tetrahedra.

t: Notebook entry and the Venn diagram
n: The notebook assignment. Students write in their workbook a drawing of the Marsh apparatus and the chemical equations of the reactions that take place in it. The Venn diagram is provided for comparing the Sanger–Black and Marsh methods, and for now it is empty. The similar and differing items of equipment of the two methods are filled in the intersecting circles.

t: Sanger–Black and Marsh: the Venn diagram
n: We compare the Sanger–Black and Marsh methods. The Venn diagram is given empty in the book. In both methods copper-coated zinc, acid and SnCl2 are used. The differences are as follows: in Sanger–Black, 2 ml of mineralisate and HgBr2 paper are used; in Marsh, 20 ml of mineralisate, the arsine flame and the mirror are used. In the table the equipment for each method is shown separately.

The general course of arsenic analysis. If the Sanger–Black reaction is negative, the examination is stopped. In the Marsh method the purity of the reagents is checked first, then the mineralisate is added dropwise over one hour. Signs of arsine: a bluish-green flame, an onion smell, a grey mirror and black turbidity in AgNO3; the white deposits appear as crystals under the microscope.

In the Marsh method the control test and the sample are compared. In the control test, with pure reagents, no brown-grey mirror should form in the cooled part after one hour. The absence of a mirror shows that the reagents used are pure from the forensic chemistry point of view. If arsine is present in the mineralisate sample, a bluish-green flame, a garlic smell and a shiny grey mirror appear at the end of the tube.

Assignments to be written in the notebook. The chemical equation of the Sanger–Black reaction is written; if the reaction is negative, the examination is stopped. Students write in their workbook a drawing of the Marsh apparatus and the equations of the reactions taking place in it. In the cluster training, the toxicological significance of arsenic and the methods of analysis are presented in the form of a diagram. The table gives the book pages: 212, 213 and 214.

The timetable of the processes. The Sanger–Black apparatus is left for 30–40 minutes. In the Marsh method hydrogen displaces air for 15–20 minutes; the control test and the dropwise addition of the mineralisate last one hour. In destruction, the mixture is left for 10–15 minutes until the nitrogen oxides stop, then heated on a water bath for 20 minutes. In nephelometry, mixing lasts 30 minutes.

Now destruction for mercury. 20 g each of minced liver and kidney are placed separately in 300 ml flasks. 10 ml of water, 1 ml of ethyl alcohol and 10 ml of concentrated nitric acid are added. Then 10 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid is added carefully, drop by drop, with constant stirring. The mixture is left at room temperature for 10–15 minutes.

The key values of destruction. 20 g of minced liver and kidney are placed separately in 300 ml flasks. To them are added 10 ml of water, 1 ml of ethyl alcohol, 10 ml of concentrated HNO3, then, dropwise, 10 ml of concentrated H2SO4. The mixture is heated on a water bath for 20 minutes. After the destruction product has cooled, it is made up to volume with purified water in a 200 ml volumetric flask.

Blitz task: write down correctly the sequence of destruction of a bio-object with sulphuric and nitric acids, 8 stages in total. First, mincing and placing in a 300 ml flask. Then water, alcohol and HNO3 are added, after which H2SO4 is added dropwise and the mixture is left at room temperature. After that, heating on a boiling water bath for 20 minutes, filtration while hot and transfer to a 200 ml volumetric flask are carried out.

The analytical course for mercury. The liver and kidney are destroyed; the finished destruction product is left with the department laboratory technician until the next session. Mercury in the destruction product is determined by the nephelometric method with a copper(I) iodide suspension. The precipitate is washed with iodine solution, and the amount of mercury is determined in colorimetric tubes. The chain is as follows: 20 g of liver or kidney, destruction, 200 ml of destruction product, CuI suspension for 30 minutes, then iodine solution and colorimetry.

Heating and filtration in destruction. After the sulphuric acid has been added, the mixture is left at room temperature for 10–15 minutes until the release of nitrogen oxides stops, then heated on a boiling water bath for 20 minutes. If the reaction proceeds too fast, 30–50 ml of boiling water is added to the flask. The destruction product is mixed with twice its volume of hot water and filtered through a double layer of filter paper. The precipitate is washed 3–4 times with hot water, and the washings are added to the filtrate. After the destruction product has cooled, it is made up to volume in a 200 ml volumetric flask.

t: Methods of analysing mercury in the destruction product
n: The qualitative and quantitative determination of mercury is carried out by two methods: the nephelometric method, with copper(I) iodide, and the photometric method with dithizone. In the nephelometric method, reagents are added to an exact volume of the destruction product; their composition is given below. As the table shows, the nephelometric method is based on the copper(I) iodide suspension, and the photometric method on the participation of dithizone.

The reagents of the nephelometric method. To an exactly measured volume of the destruction product are added 5 ml of 2.5N sodium sulphite solution and purified water up to 250 ml. Then 10 ml of copper(I) iodide suspension is added. If the suspension turns red-violet, a further 30 ml of suspension is added. If the colour of the suspension does not change, no additional copper(I) iodide is added. Mixing lasts 30 minutes.

Treating the precipitate in the nephelometric method. The mixture is stirred from time to time and filtered after 30 minutes. The precipitate on the filter is washed until the yellow colour disappears and the pH of the filtrate is 5–6. The precipitate is washed with a solution of 0.35% iodine in 3% potassium iodide; the iodine solution may be taken from 6 ml up to 100 ml. The amount of mercury is determined from the solution: different volumes of the iodine solution are taken into 3 colorimetric tubes.

Now the case and the training. Case 12: organs of a corpse have been delivered for forensic chemical examination, and the referral states that analysis for the metal arsenic is required. Task: to carry out the forensic chemical analysis. The columns of the answer table: type of problem, causes and ways of solving it. The cluster method presents the toxicological significance of arsenic and the methods of analysis. The groups are divided into 4: presenting the topic, drawing the diagram, explaining the process and writing the chemical equations.

Case 13: poisoning has occurred. The pathological anatomical examination showed reddening of the mucous membrane of the internal organs, swollen organs and corrosive sublimate nephrosis in the kidney. Task: to carry out the forensic chemical analysis. As the title indicates, this is a case on the signs of mercury poisoning.

Review questions on arsenic. What is the detection of the arsenic cation by the Marsh method based on? What is the significance of coating the zinc pieces with copper in detecting the arsenic cation? How can the arsenic and antimony mirrors formed in the reduction tube of the Marsh apparatus be distinguished from each other? Why is it necessary to determine the amount of arsenic in a bio-object in toxicological examinations?

The second block of questions on arsenic. According to what plan is the arsenic cation detected by the fractional method? Which reaction is the main one in detecting arsenic by the fractional method, and what is its toxicological significance? What are the advantages of the Marsh method over other methods? What errors can be made in the Marsh method, what are their causes and how can they be prevented? How can arsenic oxide formed in the reduction tube be distinguished from antimony oxide?

The third block of questions on arsenic. How can a fast reaction in the Marsh apparatus affect chemical examinations? How can the negative effect of certain ions be eliminated in detecting arsenic by the fractional method? What methods do you know for the quantitative determination of the arsenic cation?

Review questions on mercury. What methods of mineralisation of bio-objects do you know? Explain the significance of each reagent used in the destruction method. What is the toxicological significance of mercury-containing compounds? For what purpose is the destruction product filtered?

Additional questions on mercury. Which internal organs of the corpse, and in what amount, are taken for forensic chemical examination in poisoning with mercury compounds? Which method is used to isolate mercury compounds from a biological object? Justify the method. How does the destruction method differ from deep mineralisation of the object with concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3? Why are the kidney and liver taken for testing for the mercury cation?

Safety and working procedure. If a flame is applied before hydrogen is fully released, a noisy explosion occurs; the test is carried out with a thin test tube. Turning the tube through 180° is done carefully; the burning hydrogen comes out of the apparatus covered with a towel. In destruction, acids are added dropwise with constant stirring; nitrogen oxides must not escape from the mouth of the flask.
